content: Rotavirus infection is the leading cause of severe diarrhea in children and is a significant contributor to gastroenteritis. Vaccination against rotavirus is crucial to prevent future infections. Additional preventive measures include ensuring access to clean drinking water, practicing regular handwashing, and maintaining proper personal and food hygiene. The virus is primarily transmitted via the fecal-oral route and spreads through viral replication. It is essential to differentiate rotavirus infections from other causes of watery diarrhea, such as adenovirus, E. coli, and Taenia species. Children, particularly those in childcare centers or unvaccinated, are at higher risk of infection. Symptoms include diarrhea, vomiting, and low-grade fever, with severe cases showing signs of dehydration, such as sunken eyes and pallor. Management focuses on preventing dehydration through rehydration measures. Rotavirus was first identified in 1973 by Dr. Ruth Bishop after years of research into unexplained gastroenteritis in children. While there is no formal classification system for rotavirus infections, they can be categorized by age into adult and child infections. The virus is transmitted from infected children to others before and after diarrhea onset, often through contaminated hands, food, or objects. In the intestine, the virus replicates, leading to severe watery diarrhea. Rotavirus protein number 4 plays a key role in the pathogenesis, causing diarrhea and other clinical manifestations. The infection damages intestinal digestive enzymes, resulting in malabsorption and diarrhea. In rare cases, rotavirus can affect the central nervous system, causing meningitis. Rotaviruses belong to the Reoviridae family, with seven major groups identified. Groups A, B, and C infect humans, with group A being the most common and widespread. Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe diarrhea in children, responsible for approximately 600,000 deaths annually in developing countries as of 2005. It is more prevalent in winter, affects children more than adults, and is more common in developing countries. There is no racial predilection. Children in childcare centers and unvaccinated children are at high risk of rotavirus infection. Immunocompromised individuals and adults in contact with infected children are also at risk. Rotavirus infection is typically self-limiting but can lead to dehydration, which is a significant complication. Seizures may also occur in severe cases. The prognosis is generally good. Symptoms of rotavirus infection usually appear two days after exposure and are more severe in children than adults. The severity depends on whether it is the first infection or a recurrent one, with the first infection being more severe. Symptoms range from asymptomatic cases to watery diarrhea and, in severe cases, significant dehydration. Infected children may also present with high-grade fever and vomiting. On physical examination, patients may appear lethargic and pale in severe cases. Signs of dehydration, such as sunken eyes and depressed fontanelles, are more noticeable in infants. Convulsions may occur in severe cases. Diagnosis is confirmed through techniques such as electron microscopy, reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction, and RNA electrophoresis. Stool examination is crucial for detecting the virus, and antigen detection can be performed using ELISA or immunochromatographic assays. Imaging studies, such as X-rays, CT scans, and ultrasounds, do not show specific findings for rotavirus infection but may be used to rule out other conditions. Treatment focuses on preventing dehydration, which is the most critical aspect of managing viral gastroenteritis. Oral rehydration solutions (ORS) are recommended, and families with young children should keep a supply of ORS at home. Medications, including antibiotics, are generally not recommended unless specifically advised by a physician. Surgical intervention is not indicated for rotavirus infection. Prevention relies heavily on vaccination. Two vaccines, Rotarix and RotaTeq, have been shown to be safe and effective since their introduction in 2006. Vaccination is the cornerstone of preventing rotavirus infection in children.
